explanation: NaN compares unequal to everything including itself, which is required by IEEE 754 and is deliberate: NaN means "this computation had no meaningful result", and two such non-results are not thereby the same. The practical consequence is that `x == Double.NaN` is always false and never a valid test — use `Double.isNaN(x)`. It also means a sort comparator written with `<` and `>` can behave inconsistently if NaN is present, which is why `Double.compare` exists.
